False as stated: Serre's open-image theorem requires $E$ to be **non-CM**. For CM curves, $\rho_{E,\ell}$ is reducible at every prime $\ell$ that splits in the CM field (it becomes a sum of two characters of $G_K$ induced up). The page itself ships a CM example (`y²=x³−x`, Widget 6 option A), so the unqualified claim contradicts the corpus. Fix: insert "non-CM" before "elliptic curve."

\textbf{S2: Weak and strict compatible systems} --- A weakly compatible system is defined by Galois representations with common Frobenius characteristic polynomials away from bad primes and common Hodge–Tate weights, with strict compatibility upgrading this to Weil–Deligne compatibility at every prime.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S3: Potential automorphy theorems A and B} --- The main theorem for compatible systems states that every irreducible regular totally odd conjugate self-dual weakly compatible system becomes automorphic after a finite CM Galois extension, and a parallel single-representation theorem with residual irreducibility and potential diagonalizability is stated as the input that implies it.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S4: L-functions, purity, and compatible-system consequences} --- Potential automorphy is used to deduce strict compatibility, strict purity of weight n-1, convergence, meromorphic continuation and functional equation of the associated L-function, and that a single representation satisfying theorem B lies in a strictly compatible pure system.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S5: Extreme regularity and density-one irreducibility} --- For automorphic systems with extremely regular Hodge–Tate weights, Rankin–Selberg pole-order comparisons combined with potential automorphy of irreducible constituents force r\_lambda(pi) to be irreducible for a Dirichlet-density-one set of rational primes.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S6: Potential diagonalizability as the local condition at l} --- Potential diagonalizability is defined by lying, after a finite local extension, on the same crystalline deformation-ring component as a diagonal representation, and the talk records ordinary/upper-triangular and Fontaine–Laffaille criteria that make the condition usable.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S7: Residual potential automorphy via auxiliary geometry} --- The first proof step for theorem B constructs an auxiliary finite scheme from a family of smooth projective varieties and congruences to an automorphic induction, then finds a CM Galois point and applies modularity lifting to obtain an ordinary automorphic lift of the residual representation.\par\smallskip
\textbf{S8: Modularity lifting and local component matching} --- The second proof step is a modularity lifting theorem: after arranging local component agreement away from l by Khare–Wintenberger-type lifting and at l by tensoring with induced characters chosen to give diagonal local pieces, the Taylor–Wiles–Kisin method proves the original representation automorphic.\par\smallskip

Formalisation of mathematics is the art of translating paper mathematics into a computer programming language rich enough to understand the concepts of theorems and proofs. These programming languages, also called interactive theorem provers (ITPs), have been around for decades. Over the last few years however, the area seems to have captured the attention of parts of the mathematics community. We have now seen several examples of modern mathematics being formalised (by mathematicians, rather than computer scientists) in real time, the most recent of which (at the time of writing) is Tao et al's formalisation of his work with Gowers, Green and Manners resolving the polynomial Freiman--Ruzsa conjecture. Success stories like these might lead casual observers to believe that ITPs such as Lean are now ready to formalise all modern mathematics. However the truth is far more sobering. In *some* areas of mathematics, for example additive combinatorics, we now have extensive evidence that modern breakthroughs can be formalised in real time. However, I attend the London Number Theory Seminar on a regular basis, and most weeks I note that Lean does not know enough modern mathematical definitions to even *state* the results announced in the seminar, let alone to check their proofs.

The fact that number theory is still "behind" in this regard is one of my main motivations to embark on a formalisation of a modern proof of FLT. Once the project is finished, Lean will understand the concepts of automorphic forms and representations, L-functions, Galois representations, potential automorphy, modularity lifting theorems, the arithmetic of varieties, class field theory, arithmetic duality theorems, Shimura varieties and many other concepts used in modern algebraic number theory; formalising the *statements* of what is happening in my own area of expertise will no longer be science fiction. And why might one want to do this? Well, if we are to believe some computer scientists, the exponential growth in AI should one day translate into computers being able to help mathematicians do their work. But what chance does this have of coming true if computers cannot even *understand what we are doing*?
